subsubtopic: PROPOSED COMMON HERITAGE FUND TO ASSIST DEVELOPING NATIONS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should continue to work to achieve agreement on a comprehensive and broadly supported law of the sea treaty through the United Nations Conference on the Law of the Sea and that such a treaty should provide for an international seabed or ocean authority to regulate the exploitation of deep ocean minerals in an equitable manner, with appropriate roles for private, national and international entities and that a significant portion of ocean mineral revenues, both offshore and in the deep ocean, should be regarded as "the common heritage of mankind'- and used in a "Common Heritage Fund" to assist developing nations, to fight pollution, and to assist the work of the United Nations, especially in the area of peacekeeping, along the lines of the 1978 proposal of the government of Nepal.
He said: Mr. Speaker, last week some hon. members of this House were treated to an inspiring and most thoughtful address by Dr. J. F. Leddy, president of the World Federalists of Canada, when he spoke to the annual meeting of the Canadian World Federalist Parliamentary Association. 1 would very quickly report to the House that the Canadian World Federalist Parliamentary Association now has 130 paid up members, members of Parliament and senators. At our meeting last week we elected a new president, the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. McLean). We look forward to the high quality of leadership which we know this new member of Parliament will provide for our association.
I should also say a word in the way of tribute to the past president, the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. MacGuigan), who served our association extremely well for a long period of time.
In introducing my motion today, 1 would like to begin by quoting very briefly from Dr. Leddy's speech which 1 believe sets the tone for the motion I would seek support for from hon. members. Dr. Leddy said:
What will future historians think of our times? What will be their view of our stewardship of civilization . . . Ask young people in North America today what label will probably be applied to the twentieth century, and they will usually emphasize the marvels of science and technology, of air travel and space exploration, of communication through radio and television. Some will speak of a greater degree of social and political democracy.
If one interrupts this glowing litany to point out that many millions in the world have enjoyed little if any of these benefits of our century, these students are genuinely surprised and uneasy to be reminded, as well, that there have been two world wars, destroying many millions of lives, that two atom bombs were dropped, wiping out 250,000 lives in a flash, that six million Jews were killed in cold calculation in the Holocaust, and that even after the war there has been, year after year, the never-ending plight of hordes of refugees, fleeing in misery as the result of some new commotion in Europe or Asia or Africa or South America. One should add to this grim list the collapse of democratic regimes in many parts of the world, and the recurring misery of famines, remedied too little and too late.
My motion, which has the support of the Canadian World Federalist Parliamentary Association, proposes that a significant portion of ocean mineral revenues, both offshore and deep ocean, be regarded as the common heritage of mankind and used in a common heritage fund. To do what? As the motion says, it is to assist developing nations, to fight pollution, particularly ocean pollution, to transfer marine technology to developing countries and, finally, to assist the work of the
December 3, 1979

United Nations Organization, especially in its responsibilities for international peacekeeping. This common heritage fund, very simply stated, is a major instrument for promoting economic and social justice, environmental sanity and peace.
Some members may ask, does not such a proposal as contained in this motion run counter to the establishment of the 200-mile economic zones in the process of being implemented by many of the coastal nations? The answer is no. The proposal which was put forward by the leader of the delegation of Nepal to the Conference on the Law of the Sea in May, 1978, would accept the establishment by treaty of a 200-mile economic zone in which coastal countries would be sovereign and would have ownership of all the resources. According to the proposal, however, mineral resources, including gas and oil, would be subject by treaty to a sliding scale tax to a maximum of 20 per cent. This tax would be contributed to a common heritage fund.
The minerals within the exclusive economic zone, the EEZ, would continue to be the exclusive property of the coastal state in exactly the same way as a home owner's home in his or her exclusive property. In the same way that a home owner is required to pay a tax on his exclusively owned property, the coastal state would be taxed on the revenues from mineral exploration and development in its exclusively owned economic zone.
We know that some coastal states are rich and some are poor. Therefore, there would have to be a scale of contributions which any coastal nations would make. This would vary inversely with the per capita gross national product. The richer coastal nations, Canada included, would contribute much more to the common heritage fund while the poorer nations would contribute less or perhaps in some cases nothing at all.
About 70 per cent of this fund would be directed to development in the Third World while the remaining 30 per cent would be administered by an international seabed authority for agreed upon purposes. Those purposes would have to be negotiated. In 1970 the United Nations general assembly endorsed the common heritage principle. Members will realize immediately that this is not a new idea or some harebrained scheme. Referring to the principle, they said the seabed and ocean floor beyond the limits of national jurisdiction are the common heritage of mankind. It is very interesting to note there was little dissent at the time, perhaps because the resolution of the general assembly did not define the limits of national jurisdiction.
Then as the United States, in particular, and Canada as well, increased the limits of their territories along with other coastal nations of the developed world to 200 miles from the traditional three-mile and 12-mile limits, it became increasingly clear that the common heritage on which everyone was agreed at one point in time was shrinking and shrinking fast. It was shrinking not because the 200-mile limit makes huge inroads on the world's seabed acreage, but rather because it came slowly to be understood that the real ocean wealth lay within 200 miles of shore. This is because as much as 93 per
Law of the Sea
cent of recoverable hydrocarbon reserves of oil and gas lie within that margin of the coastal shelves of the world. On the other hand, what mineral wealth lies on the bottom of the sea beyond the coastal shelf is difficult or impossible to extract and will yield next to nothing in revenue by comparison to the estimated two billion barrels of proven oil reserves closer to shore. The effect, therefore, of excluding the developing world from any significant share of oil and gas revenues within 200 miles of shore would be to make the rich even richer, as, indeed, would 80 per cent or more of those revenues in any case, and at the same time to make the poor very much poorer by comparison.
If we survey the coastal regions within 200 miles of the coastal nations of the world we find that there would be 25 million nautical square miles of exclusive economic zones, or EEZs, as they are called. Should all the profits accrue to the coastal nations by a law of the sea treaty, more than 50 per cent would accrue to only ten nations and more than 75 per cent to the first 22 nations on the list. To put it in another way, more revenues would accrue to 13 developed nations than to all 120 countries of the Third World combined.
Let us look at the growth situation and the capital requirements of the Third World in the second United Nations development decade and try to reach some conclusions. In order to achieve a 6 per cent growth rate annually in the Third World it is estimated that the yearly flow of capital to the Third World would be in the order of about $50 billion. Current forecasts, however, show that based upon the average aid target of less than 1 per cent of gross national product per year which the developed world has committed to these countries, there will be an anticipated shortfall, or deficit, in the order of about $18 billion a year.
What would the Nepal proposal do with respect to such a shortfall? For those of us who think that the immediate potential of the seabed is unlimited, it may be surprising to learn that the Nepal proposal would yield only about $5 billion, or less, to the common heritage fund in the early years, though perhaps more later on. So the shortfall for the needs of the Third World even with the common heritage fund remains very significant indeed. However, at least some portion of the deficit would be covered in this way.
By comparison with these figures, we have available to us the payout figures under the present draft treaty. This draft treaty, by the way, will be coming before the Law of the Sea Conference when it next meets. If this document were to be enshrined in a treaty consequent action would generate about a quarter of a billion dollars in revenues; that is, $250 million compared to the Nepal proposal yielding $5 billion. And we are talking about a deficit in the Third World of $18 billion. This quarter of a billion dollars would come principally from the nodules of nickel and other minerals on the sea floor. Very little of it would come from the profits of oil and gas. In other words, in 1985 the proposal put forward by Nepal would net 16 times more for the common heritage fund than the proposal now favoured by Canada.

December 3, 1979
Law of the Sea
Hon. members should be reassured, in the interests of Canada, that the proposal which was put forward by Nepal and which is gaining support every day in the developing world poses no problem at all with respect to the legal status of the EEZ-the 200-mile limit. It does not bring into question sovereign jurisdiction over that zone, although 1 might say in passing that recent actions of the Government of Canada in giving up a significant part of that jurisdiction to the provinces may seriously tie our hands when it comes to future international co-operation for Third World development.
In short, therefore, the issue here is not in any way a legal one, but it is certainly a moral one. It is a question whether developed nations with a sea coast will limit their greed and be willing to invest a fair portion of the return from the earth's coastal resources in a common heritage fund for mankind. As someone closely involved in the debate for the establishment of a common heritage fund so aptly put it: "It is one of the greatest and most painless opportunities for international justice that has ever existed or is ever likely to exist."
What works against the success of such a proposal to share this wealth is, of course, greed and avarice. This is greed and avarice at the expense of the developing world. This leads us to the kind of situation which Dr. Leddy described to us in his speech last week. It is what the 1970 U.S. resolution had in mind. It is also the consideration which gave focus to early sessions of the Law of the Sea Conference. But Nepal's representative at the Law of the Sea Conference put it much better than I can. With this quote, I conclude:
If the Law of the Sea Conference fails, it will be because we, the participants in it, did not hold high the idea of the common heritage fund. We did not do that because in spile of our awareness of new challenges facing the earth and its inhabitants we are still victims of narrow, self interest. Look at the results. Most of mankind's share of ocean resources has been thrown into the coffers of a few rich countries.

speakeroldname: Mr. Joe Reid (Parliamentary Secretary to Postmaster General and Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment; Parliamentary Secretary to the Postmaster General
subsubtopic: PROPOSED COMMON HERITAGE FUND TO ASSIST DEVELOPING NATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this government most assuredly joins with the concerns of the hon. member opposite when he speaks about the abuse of our environment all across the world. In addition, we join with him in his expression of concern for the favourable and progressive development of those nations now emerging-what is called the Third World. More particularly, I would like this evening to assure the hon. member that the government would like to express its complete agreement with the hon. member's motion when he calls on the government to "continue to work to achieve agreement on a comprehensive and broadly supported law of the sea treaty through the United Nations Conference on the Law of the Sea and that such a treaty should provide for an international seabed or ocean authority to regulate the exploitation of deep ocean minerals in an equitable manner, with appropriate roles for private, national and international entities".
Canada is on record. Since 1967, when Ambassador Pardo of Malta introduced before the United Nations general assembly a proposal calling for the UN to undertake the
"examination of the question of the reservation exclusively for peaceful purposes of the seabed and ocean floor and the subsoil thereof, underlying the high seas beyond the limits of present national jurisdiction and the use of their resources in the interests of mankind", Canada has energetically supported and pursued, in the context of those negotiations attempting to promote an over-all agreement on the use of the oceans, the principle of reserving the deep seabed beyond those limits, in the interests of mankind generally and under the term "the common heritage of mankind".
Canada was among the 35 countries on the original ad hoc committee set up by the general assembly in 1967 to conduct an examination of this issue and was also represented on the new 42-member permanent committee on the seabed formed in late 1968 to continue the work of that ad hoc group. At the 25th session of the general assembly in 1970, this committee was further expanded to comprise 86 members, exactly the same number of states which participated in the 1958 and 1960 Geneva Conferences on the Law of the Sea. At the same time the general assembly decided that a third Conference on the Law of the Sea should be held in 1973 and assigned to the expanded seabed committee the mandate of preparing for that conference. The general assembly resolution underlined that a single comprehensive convention was necessary because of the interrelationships among all ocean uses and activities. At the same time it gave the seabed committee some special tasks in preparing for the conference, in particular the completion of a comprehensive list of subjects and issues for the future convention to cover.
The decision to convene a new Conference on the Law of the Sea required lengthy and difficult negotiations in light of the wide divergence of views regarding the scope of the Conference and the priority attaching to the various issues it would have to consider. Canada was among those countries-mainly the developing states-favouring a conference broad in scope and according priority to the seabed regime as against the more restricted conference favoured by a number of other states which wanted only matters of direct interest to be included in considerations. It was and remains the Canadian view that no accommodation on the Law of the Sea issues could be successful unless it was a comprehensive accommodation on all major issues. A partial solution would be no solution at all in the long run.
In the end it fell to the Canadian delegation to chair the negotiating group seeking an accommodation among these conflicting views and to bring about agreement on the compromise resolution which was finally adopted. That resolution, introduced by the Canadian delegation on behalf of its many sponsors, called for a conference to deal with a broad range of issues, including the establishment of an equitable international regime-including international machinery-for the seabed and ocean floor beyond the limits of national jurisdiction and a precise definition of this area to be included in the term "seabed".
At the same time, the general assembly passed resolution 2749 declaring principles which would form the basis for a

December 3, 1979

new regime governing the uses of the seabed, ocean floor and the subsoil thereof beyond the limits, again, of national jurisdiction.
That resolution represented a major landfall in that it constituted the first and only consensus of the international community in this field and laid the foundation and framework for the international seabed regime. In essence, the resolution affirmed the following principles:
First, there is an area of the seabed and ocean floor which is beyond the limits of national jurisdiction and which constitutes the "common heritage of mankind''.
Second, this area is not subject to national appropriation or claims of sovereignty.
Third, the exploration and exploitation of the resources of the area shall be governed by an international regime and international machinery, still to be established, and shall be carried out for the benefit of mankind as a whole, taking into particular consideration the interests and needs of the developing countries.
Fourth, the area shall be reserved for exclusively peaceful purposes.
Fifth, every state shall be responsible for ensuring that activities in the area conducted by its agencies or entities or persons under its jurisdiction shall be carried out in conformity with the international regime.
The acceptance of these far-reaching principles ranked in importance with the agreement on the applicability of a similar principle to outer space and celestial bodies. It represented a bold new approach towards a developing world order and a turning away from traditional land-oriented concepts of jurisdiction and sovereignty. Most significantly it put the general interest of the world community ahead of the special interests of any state or group of states. It is a concept holding great promise for the world of tomorrow.
Many years of work have followed these early attempts by the UN General Assembly to define principles to govern the regime of the deep ocean seabed. The third Conference on the Law of the Sea was convened in 1973 to elaborate a multilateral convention to bring into effect the principle of "the common heritage of mankind".
This country is dedicated to the establishment of such a deep ocean seabed and dedicated to that common heritage of mankind.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED COMMON HERITAGE FUND TO ASSIST DEVELOPING NATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 congratulate the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Penner) for bringing this matter to the attention of the House. I think it is an extremely important issue which we have to continue to pursue for the developing countries. If we look at it from a selfish point of view, I think we also have to support this motion from Canada's point of view.
As the last speaker mentioned, the Law of the Sea Conference has been going on in the third session since 1973. I had the pleasure of going to the Law of the Sea Conference in New York this past summer and, if anything, the surprise I
Law of the Sea
experienced there was the difficulty of the developing nations to make any inroads in gaining access to what we all accept as the common heritage of mankind. At that conference there are many pressures to gain the resources and the wealth that those resources promise to the world community. Developing nations, many of which are landlocked, have very little economic or political clout at the United Nations except in the formation of groups of other landlocked developing states.
From Canada's point of view, we have gained considerably from the progress which has been made at the Law of the Sea Conference since 1973, and we should be aware that that convention has not been signed. There are many outstanding issues still to be resolved, and until those issues are resolved we do not have any long-term guarantee that every nation in the world will recognize a 200-mile economic zone. We do not have any long-term guarantee that those same nations will continue to respect Canada's 200-mile jurisdiction over our very profitable and growing fish resources. We have taken on an obligation, through agreement and consensus at the Law of the Sea Conference, which sees Canada's management of those resources off our shores. There is an understanding that those minerals found within 200 miles are also the property of the sovereign state on whose continental shelf those resources lie. My concern-and I am sure the concern expressed by the hon. member for Cochrane-is that the developing nations are going to be squeezed out of the profits which may come from those resources.
If I may just reflect on some of the attitudes which I saw dealing with seabed mining, the attitude of Canada and other nickel and copper producing states was that they were demanding a certain ceiling and a certain timetable for the export of those ferro-manganese nodules. We were demanding a timetable and a ceiling in the recognition that if those resources were exploited rapidly by those nations which are capable of developing them-mainly the United States, West German and Japanese interests-Canadian jobs and the Canadian nickel industry would be particularly harmed. We understand why the United States, West Germany and Japan were and are anxious to mine the seabed. They are importers of nickel for industrial steel. They need those resources to become self-sufficient in their industries. Canada, Indonesia, and Guatemala were not very anxious for those resources to be developed in a hurry.
But what about the developing nations, the nations which do not have the technology or financial resources to exploit those reserves? Where do they stand? This is an attempt to assure the developing nations that they can gain some of those resources. Canada and other developing nations have a vested interest in saying that. We share wealth in oil, natural gas, and nodules which are expected to provide billions and billions of dollars of wealth to the world. We must look at that wealth in terms of how much it will cost to draw those off the seabed, to process them and ship them to areas where they can be utilized. We must consider how many developing nations there

December 3, 1979
Law of the Sea
are. There are probably 119 or 120 nations which do not have capabilities at this moment to utilize those resources. We expect they will share in our deep sea deepbed mines. This is why 1 say we do not have any choice in the matter, except to pursue an adequate and equitable sharing of those resources.
Other issues in which Canada is interested at the moment include the delimitation of the continental shelf. Not all nations in this world accept that the continental shelf should extend only to 200 miles. There are other proposals which suggest any distance off the coast of a nation where it can be shown that that shelf is actually a prolongation of that nation. There are some nations which demand the entire shelf. 1 hope Canada would not be in that position. There are other nations which indicate that 200 miles is the limit, regardless of the continental shelf and regardless of the terrain in the area. Nepal suggested that within 200 miles there should be a sharing of the resources in that area.
Also we are informed by some nations, including the United States, that there is a reluctance when the world authority and the Law of the Sea Conference discuss the matter of having a world authority to govern seabed mining activities, by which the authority would set up an enterprise to develop the capability of seabed mining and sharing with the developing nations. There is a reluctance on the part of the United States to share the technology which it is developing now and which it will have to develop to mine those seabeds. There is a reluctance on the part of the nations and the companies capable of doing that, a reluctance to share the technical resources needed by developing countries.
Within the Law of the Sea Conference there is a mechanism by which we would settle international disputes. We must continue our presence at the Law of the Sea Conference in order to see the proposed mechanisms or the alternatives to them. The Law of the Sea Conference must continue with Canada's presence and leadership. Canada has played a leadership role at the Law of the Sea Conference. We have done well in fisheries. We have done well in providing ourselves with the opportunity to manage fish stocks off our coasts. We have done well in accepting the responsibility to control pollution within that area. We could have developed a greater leadership role, and 1 hope we will in the future.
The matter of continuing to work toward an international agreement through the Law of the Sea, respecting the sharing of a seabed authority and the resources of the seabed, will not be argued by this party. Again we encourage the present government to assemble the kind of staff which was sent to Law of the Sea Conferences in the last six years to continue that type of leadership role. 1 hope the new government will see to it that Canada is prepared to fight for an adequate and equitable share of the resources to go to developing nations, more so than was done at the last Law of the Sea Conference in New York. If some of the developed, wealthy nations do not begin to compromise on sharing the riches of the seabed, it is my fear that those other nations will not ratify the Law of the Sea Conference and therefore will not ratify the EEZ, our control over fisheries, our control over pollution and the con-

trol which nations have over navigation and management of resources.
In closing I should like to indicate that again the hon. member has done a service to this House. I encourage the government and all parties in the House to support this resolution so that developing nations will realize that by compromising and giving Canada and other coastal nations access to those resources, in turn we are prepared to share some of the income we gain from those resources with the world community.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to join with the hon. member for St. Catharines (Mr. Reid) and the hon. member for Nanaimo-Alberni (Mr. Miller) in paying tribute to the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Penner) for bringing this significant motion to the attention of the House. Also I should like to say a word of appreciation, echoing the sentiments of the hon. member for Cochrane, for the comments and the address at the annual meeting of the Canadian World Federalist Parliamentary Association of Dr. J. F. Leddy, as he set in context our world community and reminded parliamentarians of our responsibility to be part of the peacemaking process.
I should like to say a word of appreciation to the hon. member for the ingredients which are part of his motion, as expressed and brought to the attention of the House. It is apparent to all of us today, as we look at our world, the hourly reports from Iran, the reports from the Middle East, and as we receive into the Canadian community more refugees, that we increasingly need mechanisms for world order. In terms of the future, one point of hope for the great multitude of our human family is the manner in which we manage and order the life of the seas.
When we consider that in so many areas now the resources of our land are increasingly being depleted, one area of hope for the future surely is in the harvesting of the resources of the sea and the seabed. I want to suggest that in linking together this resource with our Canadian commitment to working together through the forum of the United Nations, the hon. member is pointing to the direction in which we, as a nation, have been and will wish to continue. I think that this discussion in this House at this time is timely, as I understand there is shortly to be named the make-up of the review members for foreign policy and for development assistance for the 1980s and 1990s, and in the review of that parliamentary process surely the experience and the work which has been done through the years by this conference must be weighed and considered very seriously.
1 want to suggest that we, as Canadians, have a great deal to offer to the continuance of this conference with our long history in fisheries, being a trading nation and dependent upon world order and world markets. We are also a people of humanitarian spirit, and we can see in the motion that we wish to be a part of those who bring some hope to the needy in our world.
December 3, 1979

This motion is also important as it challenges us to look at our own national negotiations between provinces and the federal government, and in understanding some of the complexity and the time span of the Conference on the Law of the Sea we know just how painstaking and how carefully our negotiations have to be undertaken across this nation.
At the moment, as we are seeking to find ways of sharing the resources of oil and energy across our nation, we can understand how fearful certain parts of our nation are lest they not have the resources to meet their basic energy needs.
Similarly, this motion points us to the broader family concern in our world beyond our Canadian family, and to the same types of concerns which are being felt around our world. Surely something which Canadians and this Parliament can be sensitive to is both the time-frame and the sensitivity of these negotiations.
Many of us have had the opportunity to visit nations which are landlocked, and the motion gives expression to the sense of hopelessness of many of these nations, in Africa particularly, and other parts of the world. We have been, through C1DA, through other mechanisms and through the voluntary sector, seeking to relate, but what many of us have come to realize, and what many of the international organisms have come to realize, is that our efforts only touch the edge of the plight of these people. If we are to find some means of bringing hope, it will be in terms of the principles which are outlined through the conference on the sea.
I want to say a word about the common heritage principle, which surely must continue to be a mainstay in the negotiations as they proceed through the 1980s. It would seem that before this House could adopt fully the intention of this motion there will be need for further discussion, and this will surely come as the conference continues through 1980 on the makeup of the assembly, on the form of a secretariat which will be charged with the opportunity of carrying out the principles and the financial arrangements as they are developed.
More work will be done at the ninth session of the Law of the Sea Conference in the 1980s, and Canada will continue to play a significant and energetic part in that. Discussions through the 1980s will be on the development of the resources in the areas under discussion, on the composition and the voting of the council, and on surrounding financial arrangements.
This House is indebted to the hon. member for Cochrane for bringing to its attention this significant ongoing Conference on the Law of the Sea, and as the months pass and the new year comes this House will be receiving reports of developments, and surely will be in a position to ratify the negotiations which have been going on through this extensive process and period of time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am sorry to change the tune that has been played in this House this last few minutes. 1 have heard a lot of complaints about the House of Commons at times for its lack
Law of the Sea
of credibility, but never have we aimed such a low blow as in the present debate.
This motion ignores the facts of life on how the world works. It does not begin to tell what this really is; this whole motion of turning the ownership of the bottom of the seas of the world over to an international authority. In reality what it is is a ramp by international mining companies to put the authority of ownership into the hands of an unsophisticated authority run by the United Nations civil servants so they can exploit the bottom of the sea like they have exploited the land surface of the earth. To pretend that we are doing all this in the name of doing good to people who are less fortunate than ourselves does not bring us too much credit in this House.
I wonder if I might go back and just remind you of a few things that have happened in this regard. Every one of us here is the son or the descendant of people who left the old world to come here to get access to land and resources. Some of our folks fought damned hard to get them. We have seen this fight of ours hurt, over and over again, as stronger powers took from us what we have fought so hard to win.
I saw the British, Spaniards, and French, in the history of our nation, come out to the western world. I saw the British win dominance here. One family of the British won more dominance than the other and fought with the United States. Our history is a history of fighting back the encroachments by Americans taking over our soil.
I come from that type of background, Mr. Speaker, and I think you do too. We understand what it means when we hear people stand up and say we should give away what our ancestors fought so hard to win, and hand it out for a purpose that is not what they pretend, but is nothing else in the final analysis but a ramp of the giant international mining companies to get control of something they want at the bottom of the sea.
When this proposal was first put forward I had the honour to make a proposal to the Law of the Sea Conference in 1958. The proposal Canada made at that time was that the land off our coasts at the bottom of the sea for a certain distance out would come under the national jurisdiction of the littoral state, the state beside the ocean. That was one of the two proposals made by Canada. There were five proposals made altogether.
I reported to the House on this matter in July, 1958. Canada's motion was supported by all the other nations present, and they unanimously agreed that the rule of law should prevail over the bottom of the sea. The decision was to divide up the bottom of the sea on the basis of extending our boundaries out into that sea to the point where they would meet the boundaries of the other nation coming from the other side. That convention was ratified after 22 nations had signed it, and that is the basis of international law today, that the ownership of the bottom of the sea belongs to the littoral state at the present time.
There have been a number of such conventions on the law of the sea based on the Maltese proposals of 1967, which were

December 3, 1979
Law of the Sea
later modified into the stages of the Nepal proposal of recent years. It all comes down to the fact that these proposals were to change what the nations of the world had unanimously agreed to in 1958, that to bring the rule of law and order to the bottom of the sea and its unknown wealth of the future, we give control to the littoral states, the nations beside the oceans.
It was on the basis of that international law that the Conservative party, which now forms the government of this country, plans to give to the provinces of Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, Newfoundland, and New Brunswick, areas of this earth equal in extent to the size of Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta or British Columbia. If we look at the history of our country, at one time Manitoba was a tiny little province, and there was not enough economic base to support the way Manitobans wanted to build. So the government of this nation extended the boundaries of Manitoba, and also the boundaries of the provinces of Quebec, Ontario, Alberta, Saskatchewan, and British Columbia. We were once small little areas unable to support ourselves on the resource base that we had.
My party would like to give the same feeling of equality that comes from having a resource base, to the eastern provinces. We cannot do this if we hand away what we have offshore. How can we give equality of size and resource base to Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, Newfoundland, and New Brunswick by giving away the land that is ours by international law, in the name of setting up a common heritage fund? I am not opposed to a common heritage fund. I think that every province should set up such a fund.
What I am saying is: look at the realities of what we are considering in this motion. This proposal came in with the Maltese proposal to the United Nations in 1967, I believe. Canadian civil servants jumped on it and began to write speeches for our MPs to deliver at the United Nations. I protested in writing about the proposal, but support for it still continued. It is embarrassing for me to hear the same thing coming from hon. members on our side who apparently do not know the story of how hard our party fought to bring justice to all parts of this country.
When it became known that there was an attempt to put up an authority under the United Nations to take over the resources at the bottom of the sea, all the big mining companies formed consortiums. They knew the expense of extracting minerals such as manganese and so on from the bottom of the sea would be so great that the mines on shore would have to cut back their production and that the world's consumers would pay a much higher price for this new supply. The whole world realized that situation. These companies moved quickly to take advantage of the situation, and from that one should realize that it was a ramp supported by the international mining companies to put two-thirds of the world, which is under the ocean, into the hands of unsophisticated people- call it an authority or what you will-so that these companies could get in and develop it under their type of regulations.
Canada has suffered terribly through its mining regulations in the provinces and in the federal territories. In 1957 I
[Mr. Hamilton (Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain).)
proposed to this House that these regulations were unjust and that they were turning the wealth of our nation over to these companies. Those regulations were changed, and today when a company goes into our northern territories, it must agree according to the laws and regulations on the share it will take out. In the unsophisticated provinces, however, these companies merely have to pay a royalty and they can take all they want. That is the basis of the big fight between the federal government and the province of Alberta over oil.
I am simply pointing out to the House that we should be careful. God bless all hon. members; I know they have sympathies for these developing nations, but they are not helping them one bit. Canada takes second place to no nation in its efforts to help other nations of the world. But at the same time, no matter what we do, it is not enough. I am simply saying that such a move would confuse the issue. I know that there will not be a vote on this motion, but before hon. members bring up such a proposal again I suggest that they think of all its ramifications and what it will do to the policy and the hope of the Canadian government of bringing justice to the Atlantic provinces and, at the same time, ensuring that these resources off our shores are developed under rules and regulations made by Canadians, not by some international authority which has no knowledge on this subject.

speechtext:
This is a very important program under which an estimated $148 million will be paid in this financial year in connection with the properties of various government departments. In addition, about $110 million will be paid by Crown corporations for their property. As well, the Department of External Affairs makes grants for diplomatic and consular properties, foreign governments and international organizations in Canada. This means that the total payments in respect of property taxes this year will be approximately $258 million from the Government of Canada, through Crown corporations and the Department of External Affairs. These grants are paid free of any condition.
I am sure many members of this House have had some experience in local government, as members of municipal councils or on school boards. I was a member of the St. John's city council in 1965 and became deputy mayor. 1 would be surprised if there were not possibly 50 or 100 members of this House who had some experience of that nature. Members will generally be aware of the vital role that municipal governments play in this country and the great value of the services they provide, very many of them without remuneration.
Local government services are primarily for the benefit of real property, to help enhance its value as well as benefit people who live or work in those real properties. The federal government owns real property in approximately 2,500 municipalities, or well over half of the municipalities in Canada have real property contained in their boundaries owned by the Government of Canada. We are the largest property owner and employer in the country. We are a major beneficiary of the services that are provided by municipal governments, particularly to real property. I want to acknowledge those services now and thank the municipalities, school boards, the elected councillors, police officers, fire fighters, engineers, teachers, garbage collectors, maintenance workers and the others who provide the services that assist our property, as well as that of the other citizens of this country.
All of these services have to be financed. As hon. members know, the main instrument of municipal finance is the local property tax. Owners of private property have to pay this tax and naturally local councils feel that the Government of Canada should pay its way too for the services we receive. There are now various categories of federal property which receive local services but they are excluded from the grant program, that is, they are excluded until the House passes this legislation, if the House chooses to do so. The principal aim of

December 3, 1979
Municipal Grants
this bill is to remove and reduce these exclusions so that this program will cover as many federal properties as possible.
1 should point that section 125 of the British North America Act states the following:
No Lands or Property belonging to Canada or any Province shall be liable to Taxation.
This provision explains why we make payments in the form of grants rather than taxes because, under the British North America Act, we are not exposed to local taxation. It also explains why the established system of appeals through the courts for settling differences between municipalities and private taxpayers is not used in our grants program.
The present system for settling any differences between the Government of Canada and a municipality will continue. Under that system differences are discussed between ourselves and the municipalities. The municipality is given every opportunity to state its case and then we have to make a decision whether it is a case that we should accept. This system has worked well so far. It avoids great legal costs; extra staffing and delays that would be involved with any appeal system involving the federal government. This bill makes it clear that where a grant is to be made its amount is intended to be equal to the amount of tax that would be paid if the property of the Government of Canada were taxable property to the municipalities. If we cannot reach agreement, however, the Government of Canada eventually has to decide the matter itself. Afer all, under the British North America Act we are not subject to any local taxation at all. We are making grants in lieu of taxes and we have to make the final decision.
I am advised-I am no expert in the area-by my department that cases where the Government of Canada and the municipality have been unable to reach agreement in the past have been quite infrequent, that is, in disputes about valuation and the like. We believe that in the future unresolved differences should occur less often because this bill contains changes that meet many of the complaints that municipalities have been making up to this date.
The equality between grants and taxes is achieved by two steps. First, our property is to be valued as if it were taxable property. Second, the rate of tax used in calculating the grants is to be the rate of tax that would be applicable to property of the federal government if it were taxable property. The principle of equality between grants and taxes is generally followed in this program.
There are two exceptions which have been a source of irritation to local municipal governments and provinces, and it is intended in this bill to remove those two exceptions. The first exception is deductions for local services which the federal property does not receive or does not use. The second refers to the use of preferred tax rates for calculating grants on certain kinds of federal property. At the present time deductions are made from grants in respect of local services that are not accepted by the Government of Canada. The deductions for those kinds of services consist of elementary and secondary schooling, police protection, fire protection, garbage collection

and sewage disposal. The exceptions relate almost entirely to national defence property.
Complaints have been received about these deductions because they cannot be claimed by owners of private property. In addition, deductions create problems in cases where one local authority collects taxes on behalf of another. In these circumstances provincial legislation may specify how grants in lieu of taxes are to be allocated between the different bodies. In this event the existence of service deductions complicates that allocation and is a great source of irritation to the province and municipality concerned. It is our intention to eliminate almost all deductions from our grants. However, deductions for schooling are a special case because of the tremendous financial magnitudes involved. These deductions will continue where the Government of Canada operates its own schools or where it has worked out some alternative means of financing school services with a province or local school board. If the deductions are not made in those circumstances we would be making two sets of expenditures for the same purposes, and that would not be reasonable.
In future, deductions may arise in respect of services other than education only in very special circumstances. But in no case will we make deductions from real property tax grants for any service that a municipality is willing and able to provide. This means that deductions related to police protection, fire protection, garbage collection, and sewage disposal should be eliminated. I hope that the municipalities that benefit from the removal of a service deduction will be prepared to provide the same level of service for our property as they are for taxable property if they are not now doing so.
Second, I indicated that the Government of Canada presently uses preferred rates of tax in calculating grants on some properties. These preferred rates arise because most local governments are required by their provinces to levy real property taxes at two or more rates. These rates usually consist of a low or a preferred rate for residential and farm property, and a high or non-preferred rate for commercial and industrial property. While the Government of Canada now uses the nonpreferred higher rates in calculating grants on most of its properties, it uses the preferred lower rate for certain categories. These include employee housing, experimental farms, hospitals, educational properties, and penitentiaries. This is a bit complicated and tedious, but I hope members in the House will permit me to put all of this on the record.
The use of a preferred rate has worked well in the case of employee housing. It has not always worked well in other cases because it has not always been clear that these other federal properties could be properly compared with taxable properties that qualify for the low rate. In future, we propose to take advantage of preferred rates only where property of the Government of Canada is directly comparable with the taxable property to which the low rates apply. This is another improvement for the assistance of the municipality.
As a result of these changes, Mr. Speaker, in respect of service reductions and preferred tax rates, it should be evident that in almost all cases where grants are paid under the new
December 3, 1979

municipal grants act we are now considering, these grants should constitute the full equivalent of the taxes that would be paid if the property of the Government of Canada were taxable property.
This is really legislation that has been sponsored by the government House leader. I have to say that the pressure has been intense from the government House leader for this legislation to be brought forward. He is, of course, the great champion of the Ottawa area and a man who has waged a constant campaign of harassment against me to bring it on. Any generous provisions in this bill are due entirely to him and other members on this side who represent municipal areas that are involved.

speechtext:
Imagine, for 22 years payments have been made on self-contained defence establishments for the land plus buildings used as married quarters, but they were not used as married quarters, they were administrative operation, and no grants were paid. This bill removes that restriction.
The result of this enlarged definition, if hon. gentlemen and ladies of the House pass this bill, will be to increase payments in all parts of Canada. Along with the other changes that are set out in the legislation, this will benefit many municipalities. It will increase the grants paid on the property of government departments by an estimated $25 million as of 1983. In addition, there will be other benefits that relate to Crown corporations. I will come to that a bit later.
Some of these changes will be phased in over four years. The phase-in provision is set out in clause 15 of the bill. This clause is limited to increases in grants on self-contained defence bases, national parks, museums, art galleries and concert halls. All other changes will be fully effective with the 1980 taxation year.
The definition of property subject to grant has some remaining exceptions. There are only three of significance-structures, urban parklands, and Indian reserves. Members might ask, what do you mean by structures? I was struck by that question myself when I examined this. Structures are the most important. These include jetties, canal locks, and aircraft runways. These are some of the examples. The cost of those kinds of structures and the potential grant are very large.
At the same time, because of the nature of these items, the local cost of providing services is minimal. In all justice, can we say that municipalities provide services to jetties, canal locks, or aircraft runways? Of course they don't. If grants were paid, they would in most cases greatly exceed any costs to local government for providing services to those kinds of structures, so they are not included.
In addition, whereas all jurisdictions apply their property taxes to land and buildings, there is a great deal of difference with respect to structures. Many types of structures are taxed only in some parts of Canada and not in others. In addition, many structures are by nature owned only by governments. Therefore, we have no comparison to the private sector. The decision to exclude structures from this bill was taken in view of those kinds of considerations. Schedule II of the bill sets out a list of structures of which I have given some examples. That list is not exhaustive but it shows the kinds of properties that are included.
Second, urban parklands were excluded on the grounds that that property, urban parkland, provides a service that normally is provided by an urban municipality. In other words, if the Government of Canada has urban parkland, that is ordinarily the kind of service that the municipality should provide. Where it is provided by a municipality, the municipality does
not get any direct revenue from the urban parkland because it cannot tax itself. If we are providing the same kind of service, why should we pay a grant on this kind of property where we are providing the service to the municipality? That is the reason for this second exemption.
Indian reserves are a special case. I must say I have no direct experience in this because we have no Indian reserves in my home province of Newfoundland. In some parts of Canada, municipal boundaries are drawn in such a way as to exclude reserves. In other parts of Canada, Indian reserves are within municipal boundaries. However, the payment of grants to the municipalities concerned would imply some degree of integration between the reserve and the municipality in the provision of services which seldom exists.
There are some very special cases in defining federal property. I will just refer to one category because of its importance. That is Crown property administered by a federal department but leased to or occupied by a third party. In most cases, the third party is taxable by the municipality with respect to its occupancy of the property. The amount of the tax payable is exactly the same as it would be if he were the owner of the property. In most of those cases, the occupant pays the tax for which he is liable and there is no problem. However, if for any reason the occupant does not pay his tax, the municipality then has a problem as to how it enforces the collection of their tax. Normally they can seize a property and sell it, but they cannot seize Crown land and sell it. The existing act tries to deal with that problem by excluding leased property from grant if the occupant is taxable, but permitting the minister to include the property by prescription.
There have been many controversies over the years as to whether this particular property or that should be prescribed. Well, this problem has been examined at length by the government as well as by its predecessor. The most basic conclusions which emerged were the following: first, in general the government ought not to pay grants with respect to property which it does not occupy. In particular, we should continue our policy of not paying grants on behalf of applicants who are themselves tax exempt. This occurs where a departmental property is occupied by a province, municipality or school board. 1 mean, if our property is occupied by a province, municipality or school board, and they are tax exempt, surely there is no reason we should pay the tax although the organization concerned does not. If a municipality is unable to derive revenues from a body where it owns property, thee is no strong reason why it should derive taxes from the federal government when that body occupies federal property.
Second, where the lessee or occupant of departmental property is taxable in respect of his occupancy the government ought not, in most cases, to include the property in its grants. The occupant should continue to pay the taxes for which he is liable. This works well in most cases, but there would be great difficulties if we were to attempt to pay on behalf of the

December 3, 1979

occupant, particularly where occupancy is for commercial or industrial use.
There are some instances where the occupant of departmental property is taxable and where the system does not work well if the municipality seeks to tax him. This occurs most often in the case of residential and farm property. If there are a large number of problems of this kind in a particular municipality it might face the possibility of a significant revenue loss because of the difficulty of enforcing collection of its taxes. There are other instances when the federal government expropriates or purchases property with outstanding leases, including commercial or industrial leases, and when payment of tax by the lessee would mean he is paying twice- once directly and a second time indirectly through his rent. The government should continue its present policy of including these categories of leased property in its grants and should, in almost all cases, take the necessary steps to recover its costs through rental charges. The municipality then forgoes its right to tax the occupant.
The problem of leased property calls for maximum flexibility, and the act should give the minister power through regulations to determine how property which is leased or occupied by a third party should be treated in an effort to meet special cases. Then, of course, we shall have to keep the case of leased properties under periodic review.
Well, Mr. Speaker, those conclusions are reflected in the bill before us. In particular, clause 8(1 )(e) gives the governor in council authority to make regulations prescribing particular categories of leased or occupied property as being eligible for grant. We intend to have the necessary regulations prepared to enable us to pay grants on those categories of lease or occupancy which are included in grants under the existing act. This bill will require that the regulation be published in the Canada Gazette. I might say that that has not been the case in the legislation up to now.
I would point out that clause 8(3) requires that all regulations proposed by the governor in council under 8(1) are to be published in the Canada Gazette and shall not become effective until a reasonable opportunity is given to interested parties to make representations about them to the minister. That is another new departure.
I would also call the attention of hon. members to clause 10. This authorizes the minister to enter into bilateral agreements with the provinces respecting leased property. We do not intend at the present time to seek such agreements. However, this provision might be useful in the future if it were ever considered desirable to pay grants on a broader range of leased properties.
Most of my comments up to now have related to grants in lieu of real property tax. As we all know, this is the tax which municipalities levy each year upon owners of real property, based upon the value of the property occupied and the tax rate applied to that value. There are other taxes levied upon owners' real property and these, too, will be covered by the bill. Such taxes are based upon some characteristic of property other than its value. Usually such taxes are tied to the frontage
Municipal Grants
or area of land concerned, or to a building on the land. Local improvements are the best known example. The bill defines these other taxes as frontage or area taxes and provides for payments in respect of them.
Grants in respect of most of these have been paid in recent years, but apart from local improvements this has been done pursuant to special wording added to the municipal grants vote of Parliament and not through the act itself. However, it has not been possible in the past to pay grants where such taxes were levied to finance non-capital services such as street oiling. The present bill removes that restriction. Now street oiling is not of much importance in areas where all the streets are paved, but for people living in areas such as certain places in Newfoundland where street oiling is important, this can be important. I am sure the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey) would agree.

speechtext:
It is shocking to be interrupted by an old veteran of the House like that.
The bill also removes a long-standing restriction in respect of water taxes. Most municipalities finance water as a service charge but there are some, mainly in the province of Quebec, which finance it in part by a property tax.
The bill does not provide for the payment of grants in lieu of business occupancy taxes on departmental property. I know this is an issue with many municipalities; they claim we should pay grants in lieu of business occupancy taxes, but we just cannot see that proposition. The payment of business tax grants has been considered-there is some validity to the argument. However, we take the position that government departments are not engaged in business. That, surely, is evident from the record of the last 16 years. In fact, the government was not engaged in business either. It was engaged in harassing business.
There are some parts of the government which are engaged in business but they are a relatively small number of Crown corporations, the Crown corporations which are trying to make a profit or a reasonable return on investment capital. So the argument used by the municipalities would apply to them, and does make some sense. The bill does address this matter and it identifies the bodies which will be expected to make payments

December 3, 1979
Municipal Grants
in respect of business occupancy tax. We feel that certain Crown corporations which are comparable to business in the private sector should pay business tax grants, but not the ordinary departments-they are not engaged in business, they are engaged in providing a service to the public. It is to be hoped they are.
Another argument against paying business occupancy tax grants on departmental property is that the money which would be required is simply not available. If we were back in those halcyon years when revenues were burgeoning, when hon. gentlemen opposite were spending like mad, when they were looking around to see where next they could throw some public money, if we were in a situation of that kind and we did not know what to do with it all or where to spend it all, we could spire some out in business occupancy tax credits. That is not the case today. We have had that for the last ten or 15 years. The cupboard is getting pretty bare, and we simply have not got the money that would be needed if we agreed to pay business occupancy grants in lieu of taxes.
We also feel that it would be preferable to bring into the grants system some properties now totally excluded rather than leave those out while increasing the grants on properties that are already qualifying. 1 want to point out, by the way, that none of the provinces now pay a grant in lieu of business occupancy taxes in respect of the departmental property of those provinces, so it ill behooves them to look at us and say that we should do the same. There is one province, la belle Province de Quebec, that has recently introduced legislation which is going to result in that step being taken in the province of Quebec. I am not sure whether that legislation is now passed, but there is a considerable change taking place in Quebec with respect to real property municipal taxation, and the province of Quebec intends to do this, but it is the only province.
So, 1 come now to the subject of grants by Crown corporations and agencies. They are excluded from direct coverage under this particular municipal grants act, but it has been government policy since 1950 that they should pay their own grants. And, since 1967, they have been directed to pay on a basis at least as generous as that set out in the Municipal Grants Act for departmental property. So, it has been a matter of policy that they pay grants in lieu of taxes.
In general that system has worked well. However, there have been cases where it has not, and there have been no effective means of co-ordinating the practices of the bodies concerned. There has been confusion on the part of municipalities and provinces as to our general policy, and in some few instances there have been bitter complaints. So, to try to remedy this situation the bill contains three provisions. First, it provides for the governor in council to make regulations which will constitute guidelines to be followed by Crown corporations making grants in lieu of taxes.

Second, it specifies that such guidelines are to provide that grants be determined on a basis that is at least equivalent to that which is applicable to departmental property.
Third, it lists schedules 111 and IV, if hon. members will check those schedules, the specific bodies which are affected by these guidelines. The bodies listed in schedules III and IV are required to pay grants in respect of real property taxes and frontage or area taxes. The bodies listed in schedule IV, in addition, are required to make payments in respect of business occupancy taxes as well. Bodies are listed in schedule IV if they are generally independent of our own treasury, the federal treasury.
I think it might help members of the House who are interested if I just outlined what the government's guidelines will be if the House passes this bill. The first principle will be this: Crown corporations are not to enter into special arrangements with local governments or provinces in respect of real property taxes, frontage or area taxes or business occupancy taxes.
Second, the grants that they make are to be paid to taxing authorities responsible for collecting taxes in the areas where their property is situated, and they are not to by-pass these authorities.
Third, the grants are to be paid in respect of any property of a kind that would be subject to grant if it were property of a federal department. However, this will not apply in respect of Crown corporation property leased to a third party.
Fourth, the rate of tax to be used in calculating a grant on Crown corporation property is to be the rate that would be applicable to such property if it were taxable property. Deductions from the resulting grants are not to be made except in very limited cases where they could be made in respect of departmental property as set out in clauses 6 and 7 of the bill.
The fifth principle is this: Grants are to be settled and paid with reasonable promptness in respect of each taxation year for each taxing authority, having regard to when the taxes are due for the owners of private property. Where final settlements cannot be made within such a time frame, interim payments are to be made which will be substantial in relation to the total grant that the body estimates will be made for the taxation year.
Sixth, grants are to be paid free of any conditions.
Seventh, where a dispute arises between two Crown corporations as to which of them is responsible for the payment of a grant in lieu of taxes for a given property, the matter will be referred promptly to the Department of Justice for a ruling, and the opinion of that body shall be accepted.
These are the principles that will be contained in these regulations if the bill is passed.
These guidelines should help to clarify the present situation with reference to grants by Crown corporations and agencies. They will be set out with precise wording in regulations, but they will not become binding until the bodies concerned or any other intereted parties, including municipalities, have had an
December 3, 1979

opportunity to comment on them. For this reason we do not intend to have these guidelines become applicable until the first day of taxation years commencing on or after January 1, 1981, not 1980.
Provision will be made for adding corporations to or deleting them from schedules 111 and IV. This will be done at a later stage, likely in connection with a separate bill. Bill C-27, dealing with the Crown Corporations Act. I believe that has now had first reading in the House. Bill C-27 concerns the control, direction, and accountability of all Crown corporations.
I should also refer before closing to the role of the provinces in this federal program. Municipal governments are the creations of the provinces. I notice that my script says "the creatures of the provinces". I remember when 1 was elected to St. John's city council that this term was used by somebody in the Newfoundland government. We were the "creature" of the provincial government. 1 took strong objection. So, harking back to that, over the years, back, in 1965-14 years ago; it is gone in a flash. As you get older, you realize we are only transient here.

speechtext: Some more than others.

subtopic: MUNICIPAL GRANTS ACT, 1979 MEASURE RESPECTING GRANTS TO CERTAIN MUNICIPALITIES. PROVINCES AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT BODIES
speechtext:
The poll has had very deleterious effects on me.
However, local governments are creations of the provinces. The taxes which they can levy, as well as the form of those taxes and the body that is responsible to administer and collect them, are all determined by the provincs. With a few exceptions, notably those that apply to appeal procedures and the definition of property subject to grant, we try to follow the property tax institutions of each province.
For that reason grants have always been paid to those bodies which had been designated by the provinces as tax collecting bodies. As a consequence we pay grants to school boards. We pay them to upper tier and regional municipalities only where they are the tax collecting authorities as designated and appointed and decided by the provinces. In my view it would be inappropriate for us to depart from that practice, or for us to designate on our own the bodies to which our grants should be paid. That is a matter to be decided by the provinces which create the municipal and local government structures in this country.
I have to point out in that respect that in some cases the provinces themselves, or the territories, collect the property taxes. This is happening in New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, British Columbia, the Yukon, and the Northwest Territories. In those cases we pay federal grants to the provinces and the territories in the same way as we do to the municipal governments since 1967. That has been authorized by a special wording added to the municipal grants vote of Parliament and not through the act itself. If we pass this bill, then such payments will be brought within the act for the First time.
Finally, in ending I want to note a number of minor new things which the act does. It permits the payment of grants for
Municipal Grants
the first time to Indian band councils where they levy a property tax. It provides exclusions for lands for which a Crown grant was never issued and for which there is no designated use, and also for general purpose public highways owned by the federal government. It gives the minister power to reduce a grant by the amount of any cancellation, reduction or refund of taxes that would be applicable to federal property if it were taxable property. There is no concern why we should not get the same kind of reduction.
While the bill authorizes grants on community pastures for the first time, it has an exclusion in clause 11 for such time as a special existing program of payments in lieu of taxes on community pastures continues in effect.
The fifth point is that the bill makes it clear that no grant is to be paid in respect of taxable property acquired by the Government of Canada for any part of the taxation year during which it is acquired. The latter is because in fact the former owner of such property is taxable for the whole of the taxation year during which the acquisition takes place, and there is no reason why the tax should be paid twice.
This brings me to the end of my comments about the purpose and intent of Bill C-3. We can all see from my remarks-and I know they are hard to follow if one does not have the text before him-that this is a complex and important measure. It will tidy up and modernize a statute where changes are long overdue; it is now 22 years since it was changed. It will bring substantial benefits to local governments in all parts of Canada and will strengthen the principle that the Government of Canada is paying its way for the services it receives from municipal government.
Before anyone in the official opposition jumps up to point it out, I am quite happy to say that the terms of the bill are pretty well the same as the bill which was introduced in the House of Commons approximately nine or ten months ago by the then minister of finance, who has since passed on to happier things in the opposition. Therefore I would anticipate tremendous support from the official opposition for this piece of legislation. 1 would not be surprised if even the New Democratic Party supports this legislation. Normally they do not like to see money spent or any increased amounts of money spent when it comes to the average home owner across Canada who hopes to get a break in the new year through another piece of legislation that I would not mention because I do not want to get on a controversial tack here. But I hope even members of the New Democratic Party will support this legislation and we get it through the House tonight. As a matter of fact, we have one hour and ten minutes. What a tremendous demonstration this would be to the municipalities of Canada of how members opposite were concerned about them, if this whistled through all stages tonight with no hesitation, on to third reading, and became law tomorrow. I move second reading of the bill.

The following question is immediately raised: does Bill C-3 solve all problems and satisfy the aspirations of the municipalities involved? The views of the municipalities have been stated by the Canadian Federation of Municipalities in a letter to Mr. Chretien and a brief to the Canadian government, both delivered on June 20, 1977. It would be useful to make a comparison between supply and demand, between the demands of the municipalities and what is offered by the government, to record in Hansard and comment very quickly a few excerpts from the second document. It is a paper which I read carefully and, as I said, I would simply wish to put on record in Hansard a few quotations so that those who read the interesting debates of this House can compare the demands of the municipalities with what they get under Bill C-3.
1 therefore quote from the brief dated June 20, 1977 and entitled "Urgent Amendments to be made to the Municipal Grants Act". The quotation reads as follows:
Through the federal program of grants in lieu of taxes, considerable revenues accrued to the municipalities of Canada. However, the program had several basic flaws. In our opinion, the federal government should pay taxes the same way as any other ratepayer of a municipality or provide corresponding grants.
That is the principle the former mayor of Quebec City, now the hon. member for Langelier would like to comment upon tomorrow. In that paper, the municipalities indicated five issues still outstanding in June, 1977, at the time they were expressing their opinions. The first issue was the difference between the assessed value and the agreed value. I quote from the brief:
In a number of cases, the assessed value of a given property (determined by the municipality) does not coincide with the agreed value (determined by the federal government). We strongly recommend-
It is still the Federation of Municipalities that is speaking.
-to correct the situation by accepting the assessed value that the municipality concerned will have determined.
Bill C-3, as the Minister of Finance indicated very clearly tonight, does not recognize that principle. Clause 2 of the bill defines theeffective rate
-as that which "in the opinion of the minister, would be applicable to any federal property if that property were taxable property". The minister said that this difference between the assessed value and the agreed value does not create too many problems. My information is slightly different.
As a matter of fact, I have been told that in 10 per cent of the cases the agreed value is higher than the assessed value, that it is lower in 50 per cent and that it is the same in 40 per cent of the cases, which still means that there is a difference between both values in 50 per cent of the cases. The govern-
December 3, 1979

merit's refusal to accept the point of view of the federation is probably based on the lack of consistency in the assessment process from one town to another. But we should like to know, and we shall see in committee, whether the problem is serious and whether there is a way of reducing-we should always try to improve the law-the total liberty now left to federal authorities which are responsible for the negotiation of the evaluation base. We should also wonder, and the minister did so, how the provinces act in such circumstances. 1 read that some provinces accept the municipal evaluation. So we should try to determine why they do so. If some accept the municipal evaluation, there is perhaps some reason for this. I also read while preparing my speech that some commentators suggested there should be some common effort between the federal government and the provinces to have precisely a common federal-provincial approach in that area. The second area of conflict which the Federation of Municipalities mentioned is the number of tax exempt properties at the present time. There is no possible ground for discussion on this subject.
